content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper explores a method for correcting typos in a "worst-case" way, in which worst case means against, for example, all mistakes of edit distance k for specified k. To me, this is an interesting problem because 1) typos do not work for word vectors, which is the most common input in downstream NLP tasks, 2) minimizing edit distance is a combinatorially hard problem, so all brute force methods are infeasible at scale. 

The paper provides a nice discussion of these issues, and proposes a graph-based method in which all words + their typo versions form a graph, and either a word is corrected by a representative word which is the most popular amongst connected components, or a softer version of this is used. The paper also describes a tradeoff between stability and fidelity (which I think is better understood as performance degradation) and discusses how this approach that really is task agnostic. 

Overall, I think the scheme is simple to understand and intuitive as to why it works well. Table 1 also looks like a nice collection of tasks, and the baselines seem reasonable. The main concern I have is I don't see how the combinatorial nature is reduced. If you are given a corpus and someone writes a typo, what is the procedure? Is that typo already stored in a database, in which case the database is exponentially large in memory? Or do you need to compute edit distances in order to create this graph to begin with, having the combinatorial issue there? If the combinatorial issue is not resolved then I don't see why this is better than just a nearest neighbor lookup where the distance is edit distance, which otherwise I would suggest as another important baseline. (If the authors can show this is a misunderstanding on my part, and/or include a much more in-depth discussion of the computational complexity of each scheme, I will increase my score.) 

My other main critique is that some things are a bit vague. For instance, I don't understand how the sentence embedding is created, though it is discussed--the exact procedure is vague. Also, I don't really understand equation (5). What is the std taken over? What is the random variable? It seems like the first term should be conditional on the accuracy of a typo-free scheme, since the task can be arbitrarily hard.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer #2 for their detailed feedback. Reviewer #2’s had concerns about the runtime of our defense, given the combinatorially large nature of the attack space. To clarify, our defense takes constant time more than standard forward propagation, and uses $O(|V|)$ storage space, where $V$ is the vocabulary used in our defenses (we use the 100,000 most frequent tokens from a large text corpus.) To generate sentence embeddings we decompose the sentence into tokens, use our encoding function to map each token to an encoded token, then concatenate the encoded tokens to form a sentence. This sentence is then inputted to BERT to generate an embedding. Since we map each token to an encoded token independently, encoding a sentence takes constant time. 

Reviewer #2 was also confused by the notation $\text{acc}_{std}$. $\text{acc}_{std}$ corresponds to the standard accuracy of the model, defined in (2), not standard deviation

content.title: followup
content.comment: Ok, but then to clarify, how can you generate an encoding function that has guaranteed worst case edit distance for each word? The exact complexity of the "encoding function to map each token to an encoded token" is what I'm wondering about.  Doing this heuristically, I can imagine constant-time algorithms, but doing this with guarantees seems like it should require complexity exponential in edit distance.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper explores adversarially robust neural encodings for text that ensure robustness to text typos. The key idea is to balance two criteria, namely (i) the fidelity of a model, i.e., accuracy for a task, and (ii) stability, that captures the robustness of the model to perturbations. The paper proposes two methods that balance these criteria: (i) using connected components  over text features and their perturbations, and ii) agglomerative clustering of the encodings. Experiments are provided on six GLUE tasks and show some promise against baselines, when using the BERT encoding scheme.

Pros:
1. The paper, while a bit too verbose, has a tutorial flow to it. However, I would think it could be significantly trimmed, as there is an "oversimplification" of obvious details. 
2. The key idea is straightforward, and make sense. 
3. The results show promise.

Cons:
1. The proposed methods (connected components and agglomerative clustering) seem very basic ideas in this context. The paper proposes hand-crafted schemes to decide the connected components. Can't we have more principled end-to-end learning for achieving robustness? I am not an expert in NLP so cannot judge the significance of the ideas or the results, however from what I read, the contributions look basic/very incremental and heuristic.  

2. The experiments show some promise, however the edit distance of perturbations is limited to one. While prior works have also reported in this setting, it appears to be a very constrained setup. Further, the baseline accuracy of the model is substantially lower (standard in Table 1) against the perturbed performance. Is this justifiable? 

Overall, the paper uses classical techniques in a heuristic way to combat sensitivity to adversarial perturbations in the text domain. Experiments show promise, however, the novelty and significance of the contribution is questionable.

content.title: Response to Reviewer # 1
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer #1 for their feedback. Reviewer #1’s primary concern is that our method is basic/heuristic, and the same results are achievable with a principled learned end-to-end system.  However, we designed TARE to transfer between different common tasks; the same encoding function is used for sentiment analysis, paraphrase detection, and entailment tasks. End-to-end training doesn’t make sense in this context. Second, as opposed to standard heuristics, TARE uses a carefully designed objective function to balance the stability-fidelity tradeoff described in Equation 14, which we then attempt to optimize. And third, TARE allows for efficient computation of robust accuracy for arbitrary downstream model architectures, which is not possible with previous approaches.

Reviewer #1 was also concerned about constraints on our attack surface. Inevitably, every well-defined perturbation set doesn’t cover all possible legitimate attacks. However, relative to other attack surfaces, our ED1 surface is significantly broader: we allow perturbations to every token in the input sentence compared to global limits on the number of perturbations in prior work, and even allow the adversary to perturb a vocabulary word to another vocabulary word. Our experiments demonstrate that this attack surface represents a significant challenge for previous approaches.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Authors consider the attacks where there is 1 edit in the middle characters of words. They propose a mapping strategy for the most frequent words. The point of the mapping is to map all adversarial versions of a word to be mapped to the same word. In essence the mapper is a typo corrector. They design the mapper by first connecting all the words that have a common edit 1 typo. In the basic version they map all the words in a  connected components to the most frequent word of that component. In the more advanced version they define a criteria based on the distance of a words embedding from its mapped words embedding and greedily merge clusters. Using this preprocessing technique drops the accuracy of the model by 10-20%. But the model is almost 100% robust. In the face of an attack the accuracy does not drop more than 5%. Whereas other methods suffer much higher drops in the face of an attack.

I vote for rejecting this method since 10-20% drop in the accuracy is only acceptable if a system is under constant attack and all the sentences are adversarially perturbed.

One downside of their method is that their mapper maps each word individually and context independent. There is no reason to have a constant word mapper. A context dependent mapper can identify whether in this sentence “aboupt” is a typo of “about” or “abrupt” since their use cases and part of speeches are quite different. If one augments the words with their part of speech at the very least one can still have stable mappings. There would be no need for such high sacrifices in the fidelity.

content.title: Response to Reviewer # 3
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer #3 for their feedback. Reviewer #3 wrote that TARE results in a 10-20 point drop in standard accuracy from standard embedders (BERT), and argued that this renders it unsuitable for standard use.  First, while the accuracy drop we incur from normal BERT is significant (on average 9.8 points) our standard accuracy is, to the best of our knowledge, state of the art for approaches that provide robustness guarantees on our class of ED1 perturbations. This is because the previous state of the art approach, IBP, is practically limited to shallower models and specific optimization procedures. We describe this in further detail at the end of section 5.2. TARE, however, can be combined with any architecture using any optimization procedure—our mapping from tokens to cluster encodings is the source of the robustness. We can thus provide guaranteed robustness using BERT, which leads to higher standard accuracy than other comparable approaches. Even our robust accuracy exceeds the standard accuracy of models trained with IBP. 

  Moreover, when we don’t compare to the standard accuracies of transformers, our numbers become more favorable. The standard accuracy for TARE + BERT on MRPC, 83.6, actually outperforms the strongest normally trained baseline presented in the GLUE paper, GenSen, by 5.6 points. It also outperforms normally trained BiLSTM + ELMo, another strong commonly used baseline, by 11.2 points. For situations where this standard accuracy is insufficient, by adjusting gamma using our agglomerative cluster encodings we can increase clean accuracy further (potentially at the cost of robust accuracy) as demonstrated in Figure 3b. Furthermore, there are settings where deploying TARE is a critical first step towards accurate, robust systems; for tasks like hate-speech detection and spam classification where even single adversarial example can be catastrophic. Due to its flexibility, we can also hope to improve accuracy by bootstraping TARE with future systems, or incorporating context without sacrificing robust accuracy.

Second, Reviewer #3 pointed out that using TARE discards potentially useful contextual information. Contextual information would certainly be required to recover the exact original word. However, we fine-tune BERT on each specific task, which incorporates domain-specific potentially contextual information into our resulting embeddings. Without this fine-tuning, performance drops. Typo correctors normally use context, but if the context itself has been perturbed deliberately, typo-correctors can behave strangely enough to change the downstream prediction. Incorporating context in a robust way is an interesting direction for future work.
